topic: database security; differential obliviousness; TEE query processing; query optimization
status: bounded literature-status correction and systems lead based on one sampled PVLDB 2023 full text plus one direct PVLDB follow-up; novelty not established
claim: Adore's sampled 2023 paper reports up to 7.4x over fully-oblivious ObliDB for one BDB join case, but its realistic operator composition is outside scope and the threat model does not hide private-enclave cache accesses. Doquet (2023) directly advances this state by supporting private indices and composed select-join under an observer that can eavesdrop on private-memory accesses. The defensible remaining opportunity is not whether any composition is possible: it is to optimize realistic plans and privacy-budget allocation under explicit leakage assumptions, especially when data/indexes change.
positive_evidence: Adore specifies three DO operators and proofs; its BDB evaluation reports up to 7.4x for one join case and explicitly excludes realistic multi-operator composition.
Adore states known SGX private-memory side channels are out of scope; the measured guarantee and speedup are conditional on the stated threat boundary.

Doquet's official PVLDB 2023 paper supports DO private data structures, range selection, FK/many-to-many join and select-join composition; its stated observer may eavesdrop on private-memory accesses.
Doquet assumes a static database and explicitly leaves updates to future work; the paper identifies selecting PDS structures and their shares of a total privacy budget as a system-management problem.
counterevidence: Doquet shows that some query composition and stronger observer coverage have already been implemented; a claim that no end-to-end composition exists would be false.
Adore and Doquet use different operators, privacy allocations, hardware assumptions, and baselines; their speedup numbers cannot be ranked directly.
No independent security audit, reproduction, or complete SQL workload was run in this review.

falsifiable_test: Implement several SQL plans with selection, joins and aggregation over a changing outsourced database. Under a frozen attacker view and fixed total (epsilon,delta) privacy budget, compare a workload-aware planner with a fixed operator/budget policy. Charge index construction, query latency, update/rebuild time and communication; report privacy loss, leakage audit, tail latency and query-level failures. The lead weakens if fixed allocation is consistently near-optimal and updates can be supported without material cost or privacy degradation. No implementation/experiment was run here.
limitations: One sampled paper and one direct follow-up; no full security or implementation replication. The candidate is a bounded systems lead, not a claim that composition or DO databases are novel.

topic: differentially private relational data synthesis; foreign-key correlations; synthetic data utility
status: bounded cross-period research lead and follow-up status update from one sampled SIGMOD/PODS 2023 full text and targeted primary-source check of PrivPetal 2025
claim: PrivLava's latent-variable FK model reports better aggregate-query accuracy on its tested census and modified TPC-H cases, but its own conclusion identifies two limiting axes: repeated noisy observed/latent marginals consume privacy budget, and small samples can leave latent-marginal noise larger than signal. PrivPetal later directly targets the repeated-EM/privacy-budget cost. This moves the useful test from generic relational synthesis toward a fixed-privacy-loss comparison across sample size and FK structure; neither paper establishes universal utility or constraint preservation.
positive_evidence: PrivLava models FK-induced correlations with latent variables and supports foreign-key DAGs and mixed public/private relations.

On California and Île-de-France census data and a modified TPC-H workload, PrivLava reports improved aggregate-query accuracy over the baselines it tested; its reported computation can take up to 12 hours.
PrivLava explicitly states that small datasets can make Gaussian noise overwhelm the signal in latent marginals.
PrivPetal's primary 2025 abstract identifies PrivLava's many EM iterations as costly in privacy-budget consumption and proposes permutation relations with refined Markov random field synthesis.
counterevidence: PrivLava frames synthesis as a one-time release whose output can be reused, so up to 12 hours may be acceptable in some use cases.
PrivPetal's abstract reports improved aggregate-query accuracy, but this batch did not audit its full experimental tables or reproduce a matched privacy-budget comparison.
Aggregate-query error does not establish preservation of arbitrary joins, rare subgroups, integrity constraints, or downstream ML utility.

falsifiable_test: Compare PrivLava and PrivPetal on the same relational schemas as a function of database size, FK fan-out/DAG depth, number of marginals/EM rounds and fixed total privacy loss. Measure join-aggregate error, rare-group error, schema/FK validity, runtime and privacy consumption. The lead is weakened if PrivPetal's advantage disappears under matched privacy and schema settings or if PrivLava remains more useful at low sample sizes. No reimplementation or experiment was run.
limitations: Follow-up evidence for PrivPetal is abstract-level only in this batch; no code or tables were independently audited. This is not a novelty claim or a broad estimate of DP data quality.

topic: approximate nearest-neighbor search; vector databases; quantization; embedding retrieval
status: bounded systems comparison lead from one sampled SIGMOD 2025 full text and one official PVLDB 2026 full-text follow-up
claim: Extended RaBitQ's error-bounded, staged distance estimator supports useful moderate compression in its IVF experiments, but the measured end-to-end winner is conditional on the index and hardware regime. Later MRQ combines projection and residual statistics and reports gains over IVF-RaBitQ on many tested datasets, yet HNSW is faster on the OpenAI-1536/3072 sets at equivalent recall. Estimator bounds and memory bits alone therefore do not determine query-level ANN performance.
positive_evidence: The sampled SIGMOD 2025 paper evaluates six datasets, including about 113.5M 1,024-dimensional MS MARCO vectors; it reports 9-bit quantization of that dataset in about two hours using a 96-thread/48-core configuration and single-thread ANN query measurements.
Its demonstrated ANN integration is IVF-centric and it leaves graph-index integration as future work; timing and recall depend on the setup and memory/code budget.

The official PVLDB 2026 MRQ paper compares IVF-RaBitQ, IVF-MRQ and HNSW on eight public datasets. It reports up to 3.4x search speedup using one-sixth the bits on OpenAI-3072, but explicitly says HNSW is faster on OpenAI-1536/3072 at equivalent recall.
counterevidence: MRQ's projection and IVF layout differ from Extended RaBitQ; the papers are not a controlled head-to-head under identical index parameters and tuning budgets.
The sampled Extended RaBitQ paper reports favorable time/accuracy against LVQ on its chosen public datasets; this supports the method in that tested regime.
No dataset, code, or hardware benchmark was rerun, and the full MRQ technical report comparisons were not audited.

falsifiable_test: On frozen text/image/audio embedding snapshots, compare Extended RaBitQ, MRQ and HNSW across the same CPU/GPU, IVF/list/probe and graph parameters, index-build budget, resident-memory budget and recall@k targets. Charge projection/training, index construction, storage, warm/cold query access and report QPS/latency quantiles, recall and update/rebuild cost. The lead weakens if method ordering is stable across index families and dataset shifts once these budgets are normalized. No benchmark was reproduced.
limitations: One sample paper plus one recent systems follow-up; technical reports and ANN library behavior were not audited. Results are a testable evaluation lead, not an across-the-field ranking.
